transcript:
This message comes from Kachava. A little boost goes a long way, especially when it comes to caring for your gut during the holiday season and beyond.
Introducing Kachava's new 3-in-1 digestive boost. Simply mix into your favorite Kachava shake or any cold beverage.
Go to kachava.com and use code NPR for 15% off your first order. That's K-A-C-H-A-V-A.com. Code NPR.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Rongan.
Flights at U.S. airlines are resuming after a nationwide ground stop Friday that Trump administration officials say was caused by an overload of older technology used in air traffic control facilities across the country.
Tens of thousands of passengers are being impacted at hundreds of airports in what was the first nationwide ground stop since January 20 of 2023.
And only the second since all flights were grounded on September 11, 2001.
NPR's Joe Rose reports that getting all of the people impacted by the ground stop to their destination could take several days as the airlines will have to reschedule flights.
This is a mess and it's going to be a mess for days. I mean, airlines have canceled thousands of flights, thousands more delayed planes are out of position, crews are out of position.
This is, you know, imagine if you had a giant blizzard at every airport in the country all at once. You know, it's like the whole system is scrambled and it's going to take days optimistically before we are back to normal in the U.S. aviation system.
A number of flights are departing and arriving passengers are being told to contact their airlines.
Travel plans for some college football games that will be playing Saturday have been disrupted because of the ground stop and those universities are scrambling to get their players to the cities where the games will be played.
DOT Secretary Duffy said he's encouraging the universities to reach out to the FAA to schedule flight times for charters.
The White House says President Trump will meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin together on the sidelines of the APEC Summit. Here's NPR's Deepa Shivar on with more.
The White House says Trump wants to discuss nuclear non-proliferation with Xi and Putin and the war in Iran, among other topics.
The meeting with all three leaders has drawn concern from Ukraine and European leaders that Putin could advance priorities for Russia's war in Ukraine, which is nearing its fifth year.
But a White House official says Ukraine is not intended to come up in the meeting.
Trump is also slated to have a one-on-one meeting with Xi while in China. A meeting between Putin and Trump alone is not expected. Deepa Shivar on, NPR News, the White House.
Lauren Boebert has lost her bid for Congress. Here's Colorado Public Radio's Paulo Zalciyan.
Boebert is among the many Republican incumbents who lost their seats to Democratic challengers.
Her tenure in Congress has been marked by numerous controversies, earning a statewide and national reputation as a political firebrand.
When she spoke to reporters on Monday, she said she doesn't blame any one particular person for the massive losses that Republicans experience in the midterms.
Republicans need to listen to voters, not political pundits and consultants. I mean, you know, I wish that more of us could have been listened to by our own leadership here at times.
Democrat Eileen Laubaucker, a retired Navy Rear Admiral, will take its NPR.
Route 66 is the country's most famous highway. It stretches for more than 2,000 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles. It's celebrating 100 years.
NPR's Mandalit Del Barco reports it's been a part of American culture.
The classic Route 66 road trip passes roadside motels, retro diners and tourist attractions, a quintessential American experience celebrated in song.
Get your kicks on Route 66.
Nat King Cole and his daughter Natalie both recorded versions of this song.
So did Bing Crosby, Chuck Berry, The Rolling Stones, Depeche Mode and many others. In the 1930s, photographer Dorothea Lange chronicled migrants along Route 66 escaping the Dust Bowl.
Writer John Steinbeck wrote about it in his novel The Grapes of Wrath, which was made into a film.
Route 66 has also been featured in many other movies, TV shows, music videos and the animated movie Cars. Mandalit Del Barco, NPR News.
The Family Dollar Company will pay a $63 million settlement, this after it was sued by the Federal Trade Commission and 17 states.
They allege the company routinely charged customers more at the cash register than prices displayed on shelves or on the website or the mobile app.
The proposed settlement must be approved by a federal judge. The FTC said Family Dollar customers had for years complained about price discrepancies at their more than 8,000 stores.
The company will establish two funds for consumer redress and also a discount program for customers. I'm Dan Roman, NPR News, Washington.
The company pays the bills and makes a difference. Their career guide covers what makes for a dream job, how automation could affect your career choices and how your work can have a positive impact.
The new edition is an international bestseller and it's free at 80,000 hours dot org slash NPR.

topics.text: Flights resume after nationwide FAA ground stop blamed on outdated air traffic control technology
Trump to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin together at APEC summit; Ukraine not on agenda, White House says
Lauren Boebert loses Colorado congressional seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher amid GOP midterm losses
Route 66 marks 100 years, celebrated for its role in American music, film, and culture
Family Dollar to pay $63 million settlement over checkout prices higher than shelf prices, FTC says
